title: The hadith of Jibril
hookLine: Islam, iman, ihsan, and the signs of the Hour, taught in one scene (Muslim)

cards: Umar ibn al-Khattab tells this one himself. One day, he says, we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, when a man came up to us, his clothes intensely white, his hair intensely black.
No mark of travel on him, and not one of us knew him. He sat down close, his knees against the Prophet's knees, his hands on his thighs, and began to ask questions.
Long ago on this path we stopped at one of those questions, the one about ihsan. Today, the whole scene. The hadith of Jibril.

teach.b: Three questions first. What is Islam? The Prophet names the pillars: the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage for whoever is able.
What is iman, faith? To believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its bad. What is ihsan?

To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. After each answer the stranger says: you have spoken truly. Umar says they were amazed: a man who asks and then confirms.
Second, the question with no date. When is the Hour?

teach.h: THE ONE ASKED KNOWS NO MORE.
teach.b: And the Prophet answers: the one being asked knows no more about it than the one asking. A teacher, in front of his students, saying I don't know, and making it part of the lesson.
Third, the signs. Then tell me its signs, the man says. The Prophet names two.
That a slave woman will give birth to her mistress. And that you'll see barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds competing in building tall buildings.
Commentators have read these in more than one way; several readings point to a world turned upside down. Fourth, the reveal. The man leaves.
Umar says he stayed a while, and then the Prophet asked him: Umar, do you know who the questioner was? Allah and His Messenger know best, Umar says. It was Jibril, the Prophet tells him.

teach.h: HE CAME TO TEACH YOU YOUR RELIGION.
teach.b: He came to teach you your religion. So in this report the whole religion arrives as questions, asked by someone who already knew the answers, so the people sitting there could hear them.

how: Muslims study the hadith of Jibril as a summary of the religion, and teachers use it to introduce Islam, iman and ihsan to new students.

games.q: what does “the hadith of jibril” mean?
o: a report Jibril told the companions after the Prophet died
the angel, as a stranger, asks about Islam, iman and ihsan
a sermon Jibril gave to the crowds at the Ka'ba

games.q: the hadith of Jibril — tap the pairs.
p: belief in Allah, angels, books, messengers
worship as though you see Him
the one asked knows no more

s: the Prophet told the stranger when the Hour would come
he said the one being asked knows no more about it than the one asking.
the stranger said 'you have spoken truly' after the answers
Umar says they were amazed: a man who asks and then confirms.
the companions knew from the start that the stranger was Jibril
none of them knew him. the Prophet told Umar afterward who the questioner was.

games.q: you're the teacher, in front of everyone. the stranger asks: when is the Hour? what do you say?
o: give the best estimate you can.
the one being asked knows no more than the one asking.
games.why: the Prophet says the one asked knows no more than the one asking: an honest I don't know, made part of the lesson.

practice: Tell the scene back to yourself, one beat per breath: the stranger in white, knees to knees, the three questions, the Hour, the two signs, Umar, do you know who that was?
Then let it go quiet, and pick one question to sit with this week: what you do, what you believe, or how you do it.

wordCard.voice: The hadith of Jibril. The angel comes as a stranger and asks about Islam, iman, ihsan and the Hour, to teach the companions their religion. Today's word.

orig.note: the three questions of the hadith of Jibril: what you do, what you believe, and how you do it.

carryVoice: Your line: islam, iman, ihsan. The whole religion, taught as questions. Go gently.
